strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: reducing inference cost/overthinking in large reasoning models via training-free early exit, which is attractive because it needs no fine-tuning and can be applied to off-the-shelf reasoning LLMs.

The motivating analysis (Section 3, Figures 1-2) provides a reasonably careful empirical study showing that 'pearl reasoning' points exist where truncating and answering directly yields correct results, giving a clear empirical grounding for the proposed method rather than relying purely on intuition.

The method (reasoning transition monitoring + trial-answer inducing + confidence evaluation) is simple, interpretable, and easy to integrate into existing decoding pipelines without additional training or auxiliary models, in contrast to some competing approaches that need extra probes or fine-tuning.

Experiments span multiple model scales (1.5B-32B), multiple benchmark types (math, science QA, code), and include ablations on the threshold, on the choice of transition token (Wait vs Alternatively), and a case study, which gives a fairly broad picture of behavior.

Reported results are consistent in direction across most settings: simultaneous reduction in generation length and improvement in accuracy, which is a nontrivial and appealing combination if it holds robustly.
weaknesses: The paper is visibly unfinished in places: the related work section contains an unresolved placeholder reference ('Table X'), and the efficiency section explicitly states that key results ('the efficiency gain analysis combined with the inference framework vllm', 'more discussion about end-to-end latency') 'will be added in the forthcoming version,' meaning the central efficiency claims of the method are not fully substantiated at submission time.

The branch-parallel decoding acceleration strategy, which is presented as a core component to make the confidence-evaluation overhead practical, is described only at a high level (Figure 4) without a rigorous end-to-end latency evaluation using it; the only latency numbers given (Figure 7) explicitly exclude this acceleration and are measured on HuggingFace without any production-grade serving stack, undermining the practical efficiency claims.

There is no direct quantitative comparison against relevant training-free/prompt-based or post-hoc early-exit baselines (e.g., budget forcing/s1, other confidence- or perplexity-based truncation methods, or the two concurrent works cited in Related Work) in the main tables; comparisons are only against 'Vanilla CoT', making it hard to assess whether DEER's gains are meaningfully better than simpler alternatives.

All accuracy results use single-sample greedy decoding, with no reported variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing, which is a concern for small benchmarks like AIME 2024 (30 questions) and AMC 2023 (40 questions) where a handful of flipped answers can produce large percentage swings (as seen in the ±5-16 point accuracy changes reported).

The threshold λ appears to be tuned per setting without clear guidance on how it should be selected in practice for a new model/domain without labeled validation data; while robustness to λ is claimed (Figure 6a), the range tested is narrow (0.94-0.97) and it is unclear how this generalizes across model families, especially given the weaker/mixed results on QwQ-32B.

The QwQ-32B results (only reduces length by 24% while introducing 3 additional errors) suggest the method's core mechanism (relying on the model reliably terminating thinking via the end-of-thinking delimiter) is not robust across all reasoning model families, and the explanation offered is speculative ('we conjecture...') rather than verified.

The 'Performance Ceiling of DEER' analysis (Figure 5) is interesting but essentially shows that a substantial fraction of early exits are harmful (red bars), and the paper does not propose or evaluate a concrete solution to this false-positive problem beyond stating it as future work, leaving open whether the net accuracy gains are robust or partly an artifact of benchmark-specific interactions between overthinking and difficulty.

Related work on efficient reasoning is extensive, but the technical novelty relative to closely related concurrent work (Zhang et al. 2025's trial-answer + probe model, Ma et al. 2025a's direct-answer prompting) is somewhat incrementally differentiated (using intrinsic token confidence instead of a probe) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a clear and well-motivated pilot study (Section 3) that empirically substantiates the existence of 'pearl reasoning' points where early termination retains or even improves correctness, giving a reasonable basis for the method.
The proposed DEER method is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate into existing autoregressive decoding pipelines without model modification.
Experiments span multiple model scales (1.5B to 32B) and multiple benchmark types (math, science QA, and two coding benchmarks), showing fairly consistent length reduction alongside accuracy gains.
Several useful ablations are included: sensitivity to confidence threshold, choice of transition token ('Wait' vs 'Alternatively'), and a generalization check on a different model family (QwQ-32B).
Fine-grained analysis (Figure 5) and case studies (Figures 9-11) give some qualitative insight into when/why early exit helps or hurts.
weaknesses: The manuscript is visibly unfinished: it contains explicit placeholders such as 'More discussion about end-to-end latency will be added in the forthcoming version' and a broken reference to 'Table X' in the related work section. Submitting incomplete experimental sections/results to a top-tier venue is a serious issue.

The claimed efficiency gains are not convincingly validated: the main latency numbers (Figure 7) are reported WITHOUT the proposed branch-parallel acceleration strategy that is supposed to offset the added inference cost of trial-answer generation and confidence evaluation, and the paper explicitly defers the actual accelerated latency analysis to a future version. This leaves the core practical efficiency claim unsubstantiated.

No comparison to other efficient-reasoning baselines is provided empirically, despite the related work section describing many post-training-based and prompt-based competitors; the only baseline compared against throughout is 'Vanilla CoT'.

Evaluation is based on a single greedy-decoding run per setting with no repeated trials or variance/significance reporting, which is concerning given that AIME (30 problems) and AMC (40 problems) are very small test sets where a handful of samples can shift accuracy by several points, undermining the reliability of some reported gains (e.g., +12.5, +16.7).

The method's generalization is questionable: on QwQ-32B, DEER actually introduces additional errors while providing weaker length reduction, and the paper's own explanation (irregular </think> token behavior) suggests the core mechanism (monitoring '</think>' control) is not robust across models/training regimes.

The confidence estimation via mean max-token-probability is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be unreliable in the coding setting due to entropy dilution from templated tokens, and no principled fix is implemented (only proposed as future work).

The threshold λ requires empirical tuning, and its sensitivity analysis is conducted on only one model (7B) on one dataset (MATH-500), making it unclear whether the reported 'robustness to λ' generalizes across other model sizes/benchmarks where the optimal exit point is stated to vary substantially with task difficulty.

The 'Performance Ceiling' analysis (Figure 5) itself shows that a large fraction of potential gains are left unrealized (red bars), indicating the confidence-based decision rule is a fairly weak proxy for true reasoning sufficiency, which somewhat undercuts the paper's central technical contribution.

The extra inference-time compute overhead of repeatedly inducing and evaluating trial answers at every transition point is not clearly quantified against the reported wall-clock gains in a fully self-consistent way, particularly for larger or code-generation models where trial answers are long.

strengths: Well-motivated approach grounded in careful pilot experiments (Figure 1a, Figure 2) that empirically validate the existence of 'pearl reasoning' points before proposing the method, giving the paper a solid empirical foundation rather than just an ad-hoc heuristic.
The proposed DEER method is simple, training-free, and plug-and-play, making it easy to adopt and broadly applicable to existing o1-like reasoning LLMs without additional fine-tuning cost.

Extensive and consistent experimental validation across model scales (1.5B to 32B), multiple benchmark types (math: MATH-500, AMC, AIME; science: GPQA-Diamond; code: HumanEval, BigCodeBench), and an additional model family (QwQ-32B) for robustness checking.

Simultaneous improvement in both accuracy and efficiency (a rare 'win-win' rather than a pure efficiency-accuracy trade-off), which is a compelling and practically significant result if it holds up broadly.

Good ablation studies, including threshold sensitivity analysis, choice of transition token ('Wait' vs 'Alternatively'), and fine-grained per-question analysis (Figure 5) explaining when/why DEER helps or hurts.
Honest reporting of limitations on QwQ-32B with insightful root-cause analysis (multiple end-of-think tokens), which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.

Case studies (Figures 9-11) provide intuitive, qualitative support for the claimed mechanism (confidence tracks reasoning sufficiency) and illustrate concrete failure modes of vanilla CoT (e.g., repetitive loops) that DEER avoids.
weaknesses: The paper appears unfinished/unpolished in places: explicit statements like 'More discussion about end-to-end latency will be added in the forthcoming version' and 'will be presented in the next version,' plus a broken 'Table X' reference in the related work section, suggest the submission is not fully complete, which undermines confidence in the maturity of the evaluation.

The branch-parallel decoding acceleration (Section 4.2), which is needed to make the method practically efficient (since trial-answer inducing/confidence evaluation add latency), is described but not rigorously evaluated with end-to-end experiments; only a partial, framework-limited (non-vllm) latency measurement is given.

No direct experimental comparison against other efficient-reasoning baselines (e.g., length-controlled RL methods, other training-free early-exit/confidence-based approaches, or the concurrent works discussed in Related Work) in the main results table — the primary comparison is only against vanilla CoT, limiting understanding of DEER's relative standing.

Overhead analysis for cases where confidence stays low and the model must repeatedly backtrack/retry trial answers is not deeply examined; this could offset efficiency gains in harder problems without the parallel decoding trick fully realized.

Single-run/greedy decoding evaluation without variance or multiple seeds; given some accuracy swings are based on small benchmarks (e.g., AIME 2024 has only 30 questions), result stability is unclear.

The confidence-threshold λ is tuned per setting via hyperparameter search, and while claimed robust, the sensitivity analysis is limited to one model/dataset (7B on MATH-500), leaving open how much per-model/per-task tuning is needed in practice.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 10-11 benchmarks spanning math, science, and code, across 11-12 reasoning models ranging from 1.5B to 671B parameters (DeepSeek-R1-Distill series, Qwen3 series, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1).
The method is training-free and simple to implement (linguistic marker-based transition detection + confidence-based trial answer evaluation), making it easily adoptable in practice.

Strong and consistent empirical results: simultaneous improvements in both accuracy (+0.3-5.0%) and generation length reduction (19.1-80.1%), which is a notable 'win-win' compared to most efficient-reasoning baselines that trade accuracy for efficiency.
Good motivating analysis (Figure 1, 2) clearly establishes the existence of 'pearl reasoning' points and justifies the need for dynamic (rather than static) early exit.

Extensive ablations: threshold robustness, choice of transition monitor (linguistic vs entropy-based), confidence aggregation (geometric vs arithmetic mean), effect of model size/task difficulty, and comparison with concurrent baselines (Dynasor-CoT, SEAL, NoThinking, CoD, TCC).
Practical systems contribution via branch-parallel decoding acceleration to offset trial-answer-inducing latency, with reported real end-to-end latency improvements (27.9-58.6%).
Reasonable statistical validation with confidence intervals over multiple runs for smaller benchmarks (AMC, AIME).
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental relative to closely related concurrent work (Dynasor-CoT, SEAL, and the probe-based approach of Zhang et al. 2025a); the main new ideas are the specific confidence-thresholding mechanism at linguistic transition points and the DEER-Pro robust variant, which are relatively small increments over existing certainty-probing approaches.

The extensive theoretical analysis in Appendix B (noise robustness of DEER-Pro) relies on strong, somewhat arbitrary assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian noise on confidence scores, specific noise models for MAD) and reads as an attempt to formalize a heuristic rather than providing rigorous, necessary theoretical grounding; it adds bulk without proportionate insight.

Some baseline comparisons appear potentially unfavorable to competitors: e.g., TCC's token budget is explicitly set based on DEER's actual generated length, which could bias the comparison in DEER's favor rather than tuning TCC independently for its own best operating point.

The confidence threshold λ=0.95 is tuned somewhat heuristically and, despite claimed robustness in the 0.9-0.97 range, is still a hyperparameter that requires some calibration per model/setting (Fig. 6 and Table 4 show it is not universally insensitive, e.g., Qwen3-8B shows accuracy monotonically increasing up to 0.95).

The main paper text relies heavily on a very large appendix (over 30 pages) for essential experimental details, ablations, and theoretical proofs, suggesting the core paper may be less self-contained and makes it harder to verify claims without extensive supplementary reading.

Limitations are only lightly addressed (e.g., Llama-Nemotron showing weak early-exit rates is mentioned only briefly in the appendix), and there is no deeper analysis of failure cases where DEER underperforms or hurts accuracy.

The efficiency claims (particularly the 'superlinear speedup' and computational cost analysis in Appendix H) rely on simplified O(L^2) attention cost models that ignore KV-cache incremental decoding cost patterns typical in modern serving frameworks, potentially overstating the theoretical significance of the observed speedup.

strengths: Well-motivated with a clear and convincing pilot study (the 'pearl reasoning' analysis in Fig. 1/2) that empirically demonstrates the overthinking phenomenon and the existence of early-exit points where correctness is preserved or even improved.

The proposed method (DEER) is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate into existing o1-like reasoning LLMs, which is a strong practical advantage over RL/SFT-based efficient-reasoning approaches.

Extremely extensive empirical evaluation: 11+ reasoning models (1.5B-671B) across 10 benchmarks spanning math, science, and code, with consistent gains in both accuracy (+0.3% to +5.0%) and token compression (19%-80%).
Strong set of baselines (TCC, CoD, NoThinking, Dynasor-CoT, SEAL) with thoughtful analysis of why each fails in different regimes, and DEER consistently dominates them.

Thorough ablation studies: robustness to threshold λ, choice of transition monitor (linguistic marker vs. entropy), confidence aggregation strategy (geometric vs arithmetic mean), and analysis across model sizes/difficulty levels.
The Branch-Parallel Decoding extension is a thoughtful systems-level contribution that mitigates the added latency of trial-answer induction, with measured wall-clock speedups (27.9%-58.6%).

Good supplementary theoretical grounding (noise-robustness analysis of DEER-Pro, computational cost analysis) and rich qualitative case studies that make the mechanism intuitive and support the core claims.
Reports error bars/confidence intervals and multiple independent runs on small-sample benchmarks (AIME/AMC), improving statistical credibility of the results.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally relies on white-box access to token-level logits/probabilities for the confidence evaluator, which limits applicability to closed-source/API-only reasoning models (e.g., GPT-o1, Gemini reasoning models) despite motivating the paper with such systems.

Although λ is shown to be reasonably robust within a range (0.9-0.97), it is still an empirically tuned hyperparameter, and the robustness range appears to vary somewhat by model family (e.g., Qwen3 vs. DeepSeek-distill), leaving some uncertainty about universal applicability.

Llama-3.1-Nemotron-Nano-8B-v1 shows notably weaker calibration/early-exit rate, suggesting the confidence-based mechanism may not generalize uniformly across all model training recipes, and this limitation is only briefly discussed.

The extensive theoretical noise-robustness derivation for DEER-Pro (Appendix B) rests on strong idealized assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian noise across inducing prompts) that are not empirically validated, so its practical relevance to the reported gains is unclear beyond the ablation numbers.

The paper is very dense, with a large fraction of core results, ablations, and theoretical justification pushed into a 40+ page appendix; the main paper alone leaves several important robustness and generalization questions only partially answered.

Additional latency introduced by answer induction/confidence evaluation is real overhead that, while mitigated by the proposed branch-parallel decoding, adds implementation complexity relative to a purely prompt-based or heuristic truncation approach.

Limited discussion of failure modes or cases where early exit meaningfully hurts accuracy (only briefly touched in Fig. 8/11); a more systematic failure analysis would strengthen confidence in deployment settings.
